SB-EDGE-NOAUTH.title: Edge function uses service_role without checking the caller
SB-EDGE-NOAUTH.detects: An edge function or API route that creates a client with the service_role key and never calls auth.getUser(), getClaims() or checks a shared secret.
SB-EDGE-NOAUTH.why: The service_role key bypasses Row Level Security. If the function never checks who is calling, anyone who has your public anon key, which ships in your frontend, can invoke it and act with full database access.
SB-EDGE-NOAUTH.fix: Verify the caller before doing anything privileged: forward the Authorization header, call auth.getUser() and check that this user may perform the action. For server-to-server calls (webhooks, n8n, Make), require a shared secret header and compare it in constant time.
SB-EDGE-NOAUTH.fix_short: verify the caller with supabase.auth.getUser() or a shared secret header.

messages.default:
Uses the service_role key and never checks who is calling.
Anyone with your public anon key can call it.
messages.middleware: Uses the service_role key and never checks who is calling. A middleware.ts checks sessions, so this may be covered: confirm its matcher includes this route.

SB-EDGE-JWT-OFF.title: JWT verification disabled for an edge function
SB-EDGE-JWT-OFF.detects: verify_jwt = false for a function in supabase/config.toml.
SB-EDGE-JWT-OFF.why: With verify_jwt turned off, Supabase lets any request reach the function, with or without a valid token. That is fine for a webhook that verifies its own signature, and dangerous for everything else.
SB-EDGE-JWT-OFF.fix: Turn JWT verification back on unless the function verifies a signature or a secret itself (a Stripe webhook, for example). If it has to stay off, check that signature at the top of the function.
SB-EDGE-JWT-OFF.fix_short: set verify_jwt = true, or verify a signature or secret at the top of the function.

messages.default:
Function {name} accepts requests without a JWT, and its code doesn't check who is calling.
Confirm it's public by design, or require a signature or shared secret.
messages.with_noauth:
Function {name} accepts requests without a JWT AND uses the service_role key without checking the caller.
Anyone on the internet can call it, not just holders of your anon key.
messages.self_checked: Function {name} accepts requests without a JWT, but checks a signature, secret or user itself. Fine for a webhook.

SB-SERVICE-ROLE-KEY.title: service_role or secret key exposed to the client
SB-SERVICE-ROLE-KEY.detects: A service_role JWT or an sb_secret_ key in client code, in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ variable, or in a committed .env file.
SB-SERVICE-ROLE-KEY.why: Anything in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_ variable ends up in the browser bundle. A service_role key there gives every visitor full read and write access to your database, ignoring RLS.
SB-SERVICE-ROLE-KEY.fix: Rotate the key in the Supabase dashboard first. Then keep it only in server-side environment variables (edge functions, API routes) and use the anon or publishable key in the browser.
SB-SERVICE-ROLE-KEY.fix_short: rotate the key in Supabase, then keep it server-side only.

code.text:
# Server only: never prefixed with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_
SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY=...

# Safe in the browser
NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY=...

messages.in_code:
A Supabase service_role key is written in this file (value not shown).
It bypasses RLS: whoever reads the repo or the bundle gets full database access.
messages.public_name:
A variable with a public prefix (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_…) carries the service_role key.
Public variables are copied into the browser bundle, for every visitor.
messages.public_env:
A public variable (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_…) holds the service_role or secret key (value not shown).
It will be copied into the browser bundle at build time.
messages.committed_env:
A committed .env file holds the service_role or secret key (value not shown).
Treat it as leaked: it stays in the git history.

SB-POLICY-OPEN.title: Row Level Security policy open to everyone
SB-POLICY-OPEN.detects: A policy with USING (true) or WITH CHECK (true) that is not limited TO authenticated, or that targets anon.
SB-POLICY-OPEN.why: USING (true) makes every row visible, or writable, to every role the policy applies to. Without a TO clause that excludes the anonymous role, anyone with your anon key can read or change the table.
SB-POLICY-OPEN.fix: Limit the policy to the authenticated role and to the owner of each row.
SB-POLICY-OPEN.fix_short: limit the policy TO authenticated and to the row owner (auth.uid() = user_id).

messages.anon_write: Policy "{policy}" on {table} lets anyone, without signing in, {action} every row.
messages.anon_read:
Policy "{policy}" on {table} lets anyone, without signing in, read every row.
Fine for public data (a catalogue, published posts); not for anything personal.
messages.session_write: Policy "{policy}" on {table} lets any signed-in user {action} every row, not just their own.
messages.session_read: Policy "{policy}" on {table} lets any signed-in user read every row, not just their own.
messages.global_read:
{count} tables ({tables}) can be read in full by any signed-in user.
Is this data shared by design, or is a membership check (owner, team, organisation) missing?

SB-RLS-OFF.title: Table in the public schema without Row Level Security
SB-RLS-OFF.detects: A table in the public schema whose migrations never enable Row Level Security.
SB-RLS-OFF.why: Tables in public are exposed through the Supabase Data API. Without RLS, the anon key that ships in your frontend can read and write every row.
SB-RLS-OFF.fix: Enable RLS on the table, then add an explicit policy for each operation the app needs. With RLS on and no policy, the table is closed by default.
SB-RLS-OFF.fix_short: alter table public.<table> enable row level security; then add owner policies.

messages.default:
Table {table} never gets Row Level Security in the migrations.
With your public anon key, anyone can read and change every row through the API.
messages.disabled:
Row Level Security is switched off for table {table} here, and never switched back on.
With your public anon key, anyone can read and change every row through the API.
messages.default_revoked: Table {table} never gets Row Level Security. Grants to anon are revoked, but any signed-in user can still read and change every row.
messages.disabled_revoked: Row Level Security is switched off for table {table}. Grants to anon are revoked, but any signed-in user can still read and change every row.

SB-POLICY-OVERLAP.title: Open policy overrides an owner-only policy
SB-POLICY-OVERLAP.detects: A permissive open policy on the same table and operation as an owner-only policy.
SB-POLICY-OVERLAP.why: Permissive policies are combined with OR. If one policy says “only the owner” and another one says “true”, the second one wins: the table is open, even though the owner policy looks correct on its own.
SB-POLICY-OVERLAP.fix: Drop the open policy. If it was meant to add a condition rather than grant access, declare it AS RESTRICTIVE.
SB-POLICY-OVERLAP.fix_short: drop the open policy, or declare it AS RESTRICTIVE.

messages.default:
On {table}, policy "{policy}" ({cmd}) lets {who} {action} every row, and it is combined with OR with "{owner_policy}", which checks the owner.
Permissive policies add up, so the open one wins.

SB-RPC-DEFINER.title: SECURITY DEFINER function callable by anyone
SB-RPC-DEFINER.detects: A SECURITY DEFINER function that never checks auth.uid() and is not revoked from anon and public.
SB-RPC-DEFINER.why: SECURITY DEFINER runs with the privileges of the function owner, which usually bypasses RLS. Functions in the public schema can be called through the API with the anon key.
SB-RPC-DEFINER.fix: Revoke execution from anon and public, grant it only to the roles that need it, check the caller inside the function and pin the search_path.
SB-RPC-DEFINER.fix_short: revoke execute from anon and public, and check auth.uid() inside the function.

messages.default:
Function {function} runs as its owner (SECURITY DEFINER), never checks the caller and isn't revoked from anon.
Anyone with your anon key can call it with rpc() and skip RLS.

AI-PROXY-OPEN.title: Open AI proxy (denial of wallet)
AI-PROXY-OPEN.detects: A route or function that sends a prompt taken from the request body to OpenAI, Anthropic or Gemini, with no user check and no limit.
AI-PROXY-OPEN.why: Anyone who finds the endpoint can use your API key for their own prompts. Nothing breaks: the cost simply shows up on your bill at the end of the month.
AI-PROXY-OPEN.fix: Require an authenticated user, rate-limit per user, cap the number of tokens and keep the prompt template on the server.
AI-PROXY-OPEN.fix_short: require a signed-in user, rate-limit per user and cap max_tokens.

messages.default:
Forwards a prompt from the request to a paid AI API, with no user check and no request limit.
Anyone who finds it can spend your AI budget.
messages.limited: Forwards a prompt from the request to a paid AI API with no user check. There is some rate limiting; confirm it is per user, not global.

FB-RULES-OPEN.title: Firebase security rules open to everyone
FB-RULES-OPEN.detects: Firestore, Realtime Database or Storage rules with allow …: if true, test-mode rules with an expiry date, or request.auth != null as the only condition.
FB-RULES-OPEN.why: if true opens the data to the whole internet. Test-mode rules open everything until a date that is easy to forget. request.auth != null only checks that someone is signed in, and with open sign-up or anonymous auth, that is anyone.
FB-RULES-OPEN.fix: Write rules that check ownership, not just sign-in, and deny everything that isn't explicitly allowed.
FB-RULES-OPEN.fix_short: check ownership (request.auth.uid == userId), not just sign-in.

messages.always: allow {ops} with no condition: open to the whole internet.
messages.true: allow {ops}: if true: open to the whole internet.
messages.test_mode: Test-mode rule: everything is open until a date. Easy to forget, and open until then.
messages.signed_in: allow {ops} only checks that someone is signed in. With open sign-up, that is anyone, and they can reach every user's data.
messages.rtdb_true: ".{op}": true: the Realtime Database is open to the whole internet here.
messages.rtdb_signed_in: ".{op}": "auth != null" only checks sign-in, not ownership.

SB-BUCKET-PUBLIC.title: Public storage bucket holding user content
SB-BUCKET-PUBLIC.detects: A storage bucket created as public whose name suggests user content (uploads, documents, invoices, avatars…).
SB-BUCKET-PUBLIC.why: Files in a public bucket can be read by anyone with the URL, with no policy check. That is fine for logos and marketing images, and risky for documents your users upload.
SB-BUCKET-PUBLIC.fix: Make the bucket private, serve files through signed URLs and add a policy that limits access to each user's folder.
SB-BUCKET-PUBLIC.fix_short: make the bucket private and serve files with signed URLs.

messages.user_content:
Bucket "{bucket}" is public, and its name suggests files your users upload.
Anyone with a file's URL can download it, with no policy check.
messages.default: Bucket "{bucket}" is public. Fine for public assets (logos, images); not for user documents.

SB-NO-SCHEMA.title: Supabase is used, but the schema is not in the repository
SB-NO-SCHEMA.detects: The app uses Supabase, but the repository has no supabase/migrations folder or SQL schema.
SB-NO-SCHEMA.why: Most Supabase issues live in tables, RLS and policies. Without the schema, neither the CLI nor a reviewer can see them.
SB-NO-SCHEMA.fix: Commit your migrations, or export the schema into the repository.
SB-NO-SCHEMA.fix_short: supabase db dump --schema-only -f supabase/schema.sql, then run this again.

messages.default: This app uses Supabase, but there are no migrations or schema here, so RLS and policies can't be checked.

AUTH-CONFIG.title: Anonymous sign-in on, or email confirmation off
AUTH-CONFIG.detects: Anonymous authentication enabled, or email confirmation disabled, in the Supabase or Firebase project configuration.
AUTH-CONFIG.why: Rules that only check that a user is signed in become open when anyone can create an account in one click.
AUTH-CONFIG.fix: Turn off anonymous sign-in unless you need it, keep email confirmation on, and write rules that check ownership rather than sign-in alone.
AUTH-CONFIG.fix_short: turn off anonymous sign-in if unused; keep email confirmation on.

messages.sb_anon:
Anonymous sign-ins are on, but the app never calls signInAnonymously.
Anyone can create unlimited accounts, and policies that only check sign-in let them in.
messages.sb_anon_used: Anonymous sign-ins are on and used. Check that policies don't treat an anonymous user like a registered one (auth.jwt()->>'is_anonymous').
messages.sb_confirm_off:
Email confirmation is off with open sign-up: anyone can register with any address.
This is the local default; check the same setting in your hosted project.
messages.fb_anon:
Firebase anonymous auth is on, but the app never calls signInAnonymously.
Anyone can create unlimited accounts, and rules that only check sign-in let them in.
messages.fb_anon_used: Firebase anonymous auth is on and used. Check that rules don't treat an anonymous user like a registered one.

ENV-COMMITTED.title: .env file committed to the repository
ENV-COMMITTED.detects: .env files tracked in the repository, classified by the kind of key they contain.
ENV-COMMITTED.why: Anything committed stays in the git history, even after the file is deleted. If the file holds secret keys, treat them as leaked.
ENV-COMMITTED.fix: Rotate every secret that was in the file, stop tracking it, ignore it and keep an .env.example without values.
ENV-COMMITTED.fix_short: rotate the secrets, git rm --cached the file and add .env* to .gitignore.

messages.secret_tracked:
This .env file is committed and holds {count} secret value(s): {names} (values not shown).
Treat them as leaked: they stay in the git history.
messages.secret_not_ignored:
This .env file isn't covered by .gitignore and holds {count} secret value(s): {names} (values not shown).
It will be committed with the next git add.
messages.public_tracked: This .env file is committed, but its {count} value(s) look publishable (URL, anon or publishable keys). Still, keep .env files out of git.
messages.public_not_ignored: This .env file isn't covered by .gitignore. Its {count} value(s) look publishable, but keep .env files out of git.

SECRET-KNOWN.title: API key with a known prefix in the code
SECRET-KNOWN.detects: Keys with well-known prefixes, such as sk-, sk_live_, sk-ant- or AKIA, in the source code.
SECRET-KNOWN.why: Live keys in a repository are picked up by automated scanners soon after a push to a public repo, and they stay in the git history.
SECRET-KNOWN.fix: Revoke and rotate the key with the provider, then load it from a server-side environment variable.
SECRET-KNOWN.fix_short: revoke and rotate the key, then load it from a server-side environment variable.

code.text:
// Server-side only
const stripe = new Stripe(process.env.STRIPE_SECRET_KEY!);

messages.default:
A {provider} secret key is written in this file (value not shown).
Revoke it with {provider} first: deleting the line doesn't remove it from git history.
messages.public_env: {name} holds a {provider} secret key and has a public prefix, so it will be copied into the browser bundle (value not shown).

DEPS-OSV.title: Dependency with a known vulnerability
DEPS-OSV.detects: With --deps: packages in your lockfiles that have an advisory in the OSV database, split into runtime and build-time dependencies.
DEPS-OSV.why: A vulnerable runtime dependency can be reachable in production; a build-time one usually isn't. Splitting them keeps you focused on what matters.
DEPS-OSV.fix: Update runtime dependencies to the fixed version named in the advisory first. Schedule build-time updates with your next release.
DEPS-OSV.fix_short: update to the fixed version named in the advisory.

messages.runtime: {package} {version}: {count} known advisory(ies) ({ids}). No fixed version is listed yet.
messages.dev_group: {count} build-time (dev) dependencies have known advisories: {names}. They usually don't reach production; update them with your next release.
